# Punched cards for control and data (`punched_card_control`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: helped by power_loom, paper, electromagnetism, census_vital_registration, binary_numbers
- Core idea: A stiff card with holes can steer a machine: where there is a hole a spring loaded needle passes through and its hook is lifted, where there is none the needle is pushed back. On a loom each needle controls some warp threads, one card is one row of the pattern, and a chain of laced cards weaves any design and can be reused or copied; to change the pattern, change the cards, not the loom. The same cards can hold facts: one card per person, a hole position for each answer. Pins dipping through the holes into mercury cups close electric circuits that advance counters, so a census can be counted and cross-tabulated by machine.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking the cards do the weaving; they only select threads, the loom and weaver are still needed
  - No agreed layout of columns and codes before punching begins, so that cards cannot be combined later
  - Soft or damp card that swells and jams; card stock must be uniform and dry
  - Crediting Jacquard with the idea; he combined Bouchon's, Falcon's and Vaucanson's devices into one reliable machine
- History: china: c. 2nd c. BC – pattern looms with the design stored in heddle rods (models from the Laoguanshan tomb, Chengdu); later the drawloom with a pattern stored in knotted cords, worked by a draw-boy; europe: 1725 – Bouchon's perforated paper band for a drawloom (Lyon); 1728 Falcon's chain of cards; c. 1745 Vaucanson's automatic loom; 1804–1805 Jacquard's loom; 1834–1837 Babbage adopts cards for the Analytical Engine; americas: 1889 – Hollerith's patent; 1890 United States census tabulated by his electric machines; his firm becomes part of the later IBM
- Read:
  - James Essinger, Jacquard's Web: How a Hand-Loom Led to the Birth of the Information Age (2004)
  - Geoffrey D. Austrian, Herman Hollerith: Forgotten Giant of Information Processing (1982)
